archetype.name: Fringe Contender (ground-and-defense)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-ranked run game and stingy front win tight, low-scoring games, but whose sack-prone passing offense and thin point differential leave its 6-4 record with little margin.

report.headline: Elite run game, sturdy defense, shaky passing, and another record ahead of its margin
report.take:
Pittsburgh is a ground-and-defense team. The offense leads the league in rushing EPA per play (0.071) and in run EPA behind the line (0.102), averages 5.06 yards a carry (2nd), and converts short yardage 93.3% of the time, best in the league. The defense ranks 6th in EPA allowed, 6th against the run, and 3rd in red-zone touchdown rate allowed (37.5%). Together they hold the ball 31.39 minutes a game and keep scores in the teens and low 20s. The passing game is the drag: Aaron Rodgers has started every week, but pass EPA ranks 25th, he holds the ball longer than almost anyone (2.705 seconds, 27th), and the line's 7.3% sack rate is 21st. The offense has taken 31 sacks in ten games.

The record is better than the play behind it. A 6-4 team with a +13 point differential profiles closer to 4.4 wins, and the 80% mark in one-score games (3rd) explains most of the difference. This is not new. Every Steelers season since 2020 has finished with positive wins over expected, usually around +1.5 to +2, built on close-game management and a plus turnover margin (+6 this year). The pattern is real enough not to dismiss, but close-game records can still swing hard in either direction.

The efficiency numbers hide some timing. The season efficiency block reflects a 6-2 team, so it was compiled before the last two losses. Those two games were the worst stretch of the year. Cincinnati threw for 409 yards in a 38-18 rout, and Philadelphia's 29th-ranked offense still won 19-16 while sacking Rodgers five times. Both games exposed the same seams: a defense that ranks 25th in EPA on deep throws and 24th in explosive pass rate allowed, and an offense that cannot pass its way out when the run stalls. The playcalling makes it worse, because Pittsburgh still throws 3.6 points more often than expected (4th) despite owning the league's best run game.

Where it goes from here depends on health and identity. Left guard Mason McCormick (93% of snaps) is on IR, which hits the run game and a pass protection that was already leaky. Edge rushers Alex Highsmith (doubtful) and Nick Herbig (out) are both missing this week. That matters a lot for a defense whose 3rd-ranked sack total came from only an 18th-ranked pressure rate. The schedule after Denver is soft except Jacksonville, with two games against a 4-7 Baltimore and a trip to 1-9 Tennessee. In a three-way AFC North race, a run-first approach should be enough to stay in it.

strengths.title: League's best rushing attack
strengths.body: Pittsburgh leads the league in rushing EPA and run EPA, ranks 2nd in yards per carry and 1st in short-yardage conversion. The line is driving it: an 18.1% stuff rate (8th) and the fewest line penalties per game in the league. Jaylen Warren carries the load with Rico Dowdle behind him. McCormick's absence is a real test, but the scheme and the backs have produced all year, including 200 rushing yards in the Week 8 rout of Cleveland.

strengths.title: Front that wins the money downs
strengths.body: The defense ranks 6th in rush EPA allowed, 7th on third downs and 3rd in red-zone touchdown rate. Offenses move the ball between the twenties but settle for field goals. That plus a 31.39-minute possession edge is how this team keeps games close enough to win late. Red-zone defense is one of the noisier stats, but the run defense underneath it is solid.

strengths.title: Clean, disciplined, ball-secure
strengths.body: Only 5.9 penalties a game (2nd) and a +6 turnover differential mean Pittsburgh rarely gives away field position. This is a franchise trait. Turnover margin has been positive in every season shown since 2019, so it is more repeatable than usual, though the size of any single year's edge isn't.

concerns.title: Passing game sinks drives
concerns.body: Pass EPA is 25th, the sack rate 21st, and Rodgers' time to throw 27th. Holding the ball behind a middling line produces drive-killing sacks: 31 of them, including five each at Tampa, Cleveland and Philadelphia. Losing McCormick makes the protection thinner. The playcalling also passes more than expected despite a better option on the ground, so part of this is self-inflicted and fixable.

concerns.title: Deep balls and tight ends hurt
concerns.body: The defense allows 0.61 EPA on deep throws (25th) and ranks 24th in explosive pass rate. Opposing TE1s gain 0.45 EPA per target, 30th in the league. Cincinnati's 409 passing yards showed what a good passing offense does with that. The sack-heavy pass rush has been covering for the coverage, and that rush is now short two edge players.

concerns.title: Record leans on close games
concerns.body: Six wins on a differential that implies 4.4, plus an 80% one-score win rate, is the profile that usually regresses. History softens it: the Steelers have beaten their expected wins every year since 2020. A soft remaining schedule helps too. Still, the margin between 10-7 and 8-9 is mostly late-game coin flips, and special teams (23rd in EPA per game) don't help win them.

trend.note: From Week 3 through Week 8 the Steelers won five of six on the strength of the run game and defense. They have since lost back-to-back games, giving up 38 to Cincinnati and scoring only 16 against Philadelphia's weak defense while taking five sacks.

nextGame.headline: Run into Denver's soft front, survive its pass rush
nextGame.body:
Denver arrives 8-2 but plays like a .500 team: 15th in net EPA, 15th in point differential per game, and 1st in both wins over expected and one-score win rate. Its offense ranks 30th in yards per game and runs poorly (3.42 per carry, 26th). Its run defense is the soft spot, 26th in rush EPA allowed and 31st in missed tackles, which is exactly where Pittsburgh is strongest. The danger is the other matchup. Denver's defense ranks 2nd in QB hit rate and 3rd in sacks against a Steelers line that already allows too many. Bo Nix plays behind a line that ranks 3rd in sack rate allowed, so even a healthy Steelers rush would have had trouble getting home. The Book has Denver -3 on the road with a 38.5 total, with Pittsburgh at +131, and the Steelers are on five days' rest for a Friday game.

Availability tilts toward Denver. Pittsburgh is without Herbig and likely without Highsmith, its two main edge rushers, and without McCormick at guard. Michael Pittman Jr. is expected back, which gives Rodgers another target against a Denver defense that has been hurt by WR2s and WR3s. Denver is missing starting safety Brandon Jones (91% of snaps), a real loss for a run defense that already misses tackles. An early forecast calls for wind around 17 mph with gusts near 39 and drizzle. If that holds, it pushes both teams toward the ground, which suits Pittsburgh far more than Denver.

waysToWin.title: Pound a leaky run defense
waysToWin.body: Denver ranks 26th in rush EPA allowed, 23rd in explosive runs allowed and 31st in missed tackles, and is missing its starting safety. Feeding Warren and Dowdle keeps Rodgers out of obvious passing downs against Denver's rush and shortens the game. Pittsburgh should run more than it has been, especially if the wind shows up.

waysToWin.title: Make Denver drive the length
waysToWin.body: Denver's offense ranks 30th in yards per game and can't run (3.42 yards per carry). Pittsburgh's red-zone and third-down defense can turn its long drives into field goals. A low-scoring game around the 38.5 total is the script where the Steelers' close-game track record pays off.

waysToWin.title: Attack the middle with tight ends
waysToWin.body: Denver allows 0.44 EPA per target to TE1s (28th) and gets beaten by slot and third receivers. Freiermuth and Washington offer quick, short targets that don't require long dropbacks against a rush ranked 2nd in hit rate.

waysToLose.title: Denver's rush swallows Rodgers
waysToLose.body: Denver hits quarterbacks at the 2nd-highest rate and Pittsburgh's line is 21st in sack rate, now without McCormick. If the Steelers fall behind and have to throw, the drive-killing sacks seen at Philadelphia return. Sacks also lead to the turnovers Denver feeds on, since it is 5th in turnover margin.

waysToLose.title: No pass rush, Nix gets comfortable
waysToLose.body: Pittsburgh's defense depends on sacks, which ranked 3rd despite only an 18th-ranked pressure rate, and it is now without Herbig and probably Highsmith. Nix plays behind a line that ranks 3rd in sack rate allowed. With time to throw, he can test a secondary that ranks 25th on deep passes.

waysToLose.title: Losing the hidden-yardage game
waysToLose.body: Denver's special teams rank 11th and Pittsburgh's 23rd, and Denver has won every one-score game it has played. In a close, low-total game, a return, a kick or a fourth-down call decides it. Pittsburgh goes for it on fourth down less often than anyone but one team.

nextGame.watch: Pittsburgh's early-down run calls. If Warren gets going against Denver's 26th-ranked run defense, the Steelers control the game; if they keep throwing above expectation, Denver's pass rush decides it.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation holds up: a top-two run game and a top-ten defense against the run are stable traits. The rest of the schedule is gentle outside Jacksonville, with two Baltimore games, Carolina, Houston and a 1-9 Tennessee. Expect more wins than losses and more games decided by a score. The parts likely to slip are the close-game win rate and red-zone defense, which tend to drift toward average. A pass rush without its edge pair won't keep converting a middling pressure rate into sacks at this pace, so the deep-ball leaks seen against Cincinnati could become more frequent.

The passing game is the swing piece. Pittman's return and Dunker's possible return at guard could steady protection. A shift toward the run the team is actually good at would make the offense less sack-prone and better suited to winning low-scoring games. With Cincinnati and Cleveland level or ahead in the division, the realistic band is a fringe playoff team that wins the AFC North if the coin flips keep landing and misses on tiebreakers if they don't.
swingFactors: Highsmith and Herbig's return to the pass rush
Close-game results in the division race

confidence.note: Ten games with stable QB play, but efficiency ranks predate the last two losses and key injuries hit both lines.
